metadata.title: Sudden death and paroxysmal autonomic dysfunction in stiff-man syndrome.
metadata.abstract: Two women with typical stiff-man syndrome (SMS) developed increasingly frequent attacks of muscle spasms with severe paroxysmal autonomic dysfunctions such as transient hyperpyrexia, diaphoresis, tachypnea, tachycardia, pupillary dilation, and arterial hypertension. Autoantibodies to GABA-ergic neurons were identified in the serum of both patients and in the cerebrospinal fluid of one. Both died suddenly and unexpectedly. General autopsy did not reveal the cause of death. Neuropathological studies revealed perivascular gliosis in the spinal cord and brain stem of one patient and lymphocytic perivascular infiltration in the spinal cord, brain stem, and basal ganglia of the other. The occurrence of a chronic inflammatory reaction in one of the two patients supports the idea that an autoimmune disease against GABA-ergic neurons may be involved in SMS. A review of the literature indicates that functional impairment in SMS is severe and prognosis is unpredictable because of the potential for sudden and unexpected death. Both muscular abnormalities and autonomic dysfunctions may result from autoimmunity directed against GABA-ergic neurons.

(SMS) developed increasingly frequent attacks of muscle 
spasms with severe paroxysmal autonomic dysfunctions 
such as transient hyperpyrexia, diaphoresis, tachypnea, 
tachycardia, pupillary dilation, and arterial hyper- 
tension. Autoantibodies to GABA-ergic neurons were 
identified in the serum of both patients and in the cere- 
brospinal fluid of one. Both died suddenly and unex- 
pectedly. General autopsy did not reveal the cause of 
death. Neuropathological studies revealed perivascular 
gliosis in the spinal cord and brain stem of one patient 
and lymphocytic perivascular infiltration in the spinal 
cord, brain stem, and basal ganglia of the other. The 
occurrence of a chronic inflammatory reaction in one of 
the two patients supports the idea that an autoimmune 
disease against GABA-ergic neurons may be involved in 
SMS. A review of the literature indicates that functional 
impairment in SMS is severe and prognosis is unpredict- 
able because of the potential for sudden and unexpected 
death. Both muscular abnormalities and autonomic dys- 
functions may result from autoimmunity directed against 
GABA-ergic neurons.

death 
Introduction 
Stiff-man syndrome (SMS) is a rare disease charac- 
terized by progressive and fluctuating muscle rigidity 
with superimposed painful spasms [9, 23]. The painful 
spasms, which involve (often asymmetrically) the proxi- 
mal muscles of the extremities, trunk, and neck, may 
occur spontaneously or be triggered by sensory and emo-

tional stimuli. Diaphoresis, tachycardia, and arterial 
hypertension can accompany paroxysmal muscle spasm 
[1, 9, 32]. However, the potential for death associated 
with autonomic dysfunction in SMS has not been em- 
phasized. We report two cases of clinically typical SMS 
in patients who had autoantibodies directed against 
GABA-ergic neurons (GABA-NA) [6, 33]. Both pa- 
tients died suddenly and unexpectedly in the course of 
severe and frequent attacks of muscle spasms associated 
with marked paroxysmal autonomic hyperactivity. 
Case reports 
Case 1 
A 40-year-old woman with poorly controlled insulin-dependent di- 
abetes mellitus had a diagnosis of "spinal seizures" and was trans- 
ferred to the Cleveland Clinic Hospital. Approximately 6 years 
earlier she had developed occasional spasms in her back and right 
leg, which gradually worsened. One year prior to admission she 
had experienced progressive, sustained rigidity with involuntary 
jerking and severe, painful extensor spasms of both lower extrem- 
ities, lasting up to 5 min and occurring many times a day. Her daily 
medication on admission included NPH insulin (26 units), oral 
ranitidine (150 mg), oral diazepam (10 mg × 3), propoxyphene 
(200 mg× 6), valproic acid (250 mg x 4), phenytoin (400 mg), and 
clonazepam (1 mg × 3). 
Physical examination showed normal vital signs, prominent 
lumbar lordosis, and marked distress with spontaneous painful 
extensor spasms of her lower extremities and opisthotonic postur- 
ing. Neurological examination showed sustained stiffness of her 
trunk and lower extremities and hyper-reflexia with extensor plan- 
tar responses, but no definite muscle weakness. Passive movement 
of her legs triggered painful leg spasms. She was unable to sit or 
stand without support. The rest of a complete neurological exami- 
nation was unremarkable. 
Laboratory studies showed fasting blood sugar levels varying 
from 160 mg/dl to 320 mg/dl and a glycosylated hemoglobin level 
of 9.8% (normal 3.5-6.5%). Liver function tests showed changes 
consistent with mild drug-induced hepatitis. Creatine kinase level 
was 1,168 IU/1 (normal 20-180 IU/1) with a 99% MM fraction. 
Sedimentation rate and other acute reactive substances were mod- 
erately elevated. The results of other studies (blood chemistry,

92 
complete blood counts, serological tests, HIV test, endocrine func- 
tion, and screening for heavy metals) were normal or negative. 
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies of the head and spinal 
cord showed only lumbar lordosis. General anesthesia was re- 
quired to perform lumbar puncture for a cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) 
analysis; the findings were normal. Electroencephalography 
(EEG) and electromyography (EMG) with motor and sensory 
nerve conduction studies were normal. The needle electrode ex- 
amination revealed continuous muscle fiber activity and full inter- 
ference pattern in the involved muscles during typical muscle 
spasms. There was no evidence of myopathic or neurogenic motor 
unit changes. 
During hospitalization, she required more diazepam (up to 
100 mg/day) to relieve severe painful spasms, which accompanied 
autonomic hyperactivity that included elevated blood pressure, 
tachycardia, and diaphoresis. With an intravenous amobarbital 
injection the patient became able to walk with minimal support. 
Underlying psychopathology and chemical dependency were sus- 
pected as contributing to her symptoms. Diazepam was slowly ta- 
pered to 40 mg/day over 2 weeks. She developed more frequent at- 
tacks of painful spasms and more striking episodes of autonomic 
hyperactivity, including diaphoresis, piloerection, tachycardia to 
160/min, tachypnea to 32/min, pupillary dilation, agitation, hyper- 
pyrexia to 38.6°C, and arterial hypertension to 230/100 mmHg. 
Basal serum norepinephrine was 8,337 ng/1 (normal 34-402 ng/1) 
and basal epinephrine was 460 ng/1 (normal 17-78 ng/l). A 
clonidine suppression test did not alter catecholamine levels. An 
abdominal computed tomography scan was normal. In addition to 
diazepam, propranolol, clonidine, and thorazine were adminis- 
tered in an attempt to suppress the autonomic episodes. One of 
her attacks was accompanied by a 90-s period of apnea and 
cyanosis. Paroxysmal attacks of autonomic hyperactivity and ex- 
tensor leg spasms continued. The patient was found dead on the 
54th day of hospitalization. 
General autopsy showed aspiration pneumonia and an inciden- 
tal small non-obstructing right atrial myxoma. No pheochromo- 
cytoma was found, and no abnormalities of the cardiac conduction 
system were present. Gross examination showed that the brain and 
spinal cord were normal. Microscopic examination revealed focal 
perivascu/ar gliosis throughout in lower brain stem and spinal cord 
(Fig. 1). There were occasional anterior horn cells with central 
chromatolysis at the lumbar segment. However, the intermedio- 
lateral nucleus and hypothalamus were histologically normal. The 
autonomic ganglia were not examined.

with perivascular gliosis (arrow). Hematoxytine and eosin stain, 
x 180 
Fig,2. Section of the thoracic spinal cord of case 2 shows peri- 
vascular lymphocytic infiltration (arrow). Modified Kluver-Barrer 
stain, x 190 
Case 2 
A 43-year-old woman developed episodes of painful muscle 
spasms in her lower back and legs 8 years before admission to the 
Cleveland Clinic Hospital. She was initially treated with diazepam 
(5 mg × 3) daily. Four years prior to admission, the frequency of 
her attacks had increased to 5-10/day, of up to 30 min each. 
Ambulation became difficult; 2 years before admission she had be- 
come mostly wheelchair-bound. She had intermittent diplopia, 
blurred vision, dysphagia, and a weight loss of 18 kg. She had been 
receiving baclofen (10 mg × 3) and diazepam (5 mg × 3) daily for 
l year before admission. 
Physical examination showed normal vital signs, lumbar 
lordosis, and grade 2/6 systolic ejection heart murmur. She was in 
severe distress, with intermittent painful spasms. Her trunk and 
lower extremity muscles showed board-like rigidity. Sensory 
stimuli such as touching of the skin or passive stretching of the ex- 
tremity would trigger painful extensor spasms. Muscle strength 
testing was difficult to perform but showed no definite weakness. 
Neuro-ophthalmological abnormalities included light/near accom- 
modation dissociation of pupillary responses, limited upward gaze, 
bilateral slow saccadic eye movements, occasional lid retraction, 
and decreased eye blinking. She was able to stand when aided by 
two assistants, but had a stooped and flexed posture. The remain- 
der of a complete neurological examination was unremarkable. 
CSF analysis revealed an abnormal IgG index (0.77; normal 
value <_ 0.70) and several oligocloncal bands. Extensive laboratory 
studies revealed only a mild iron-deficiency anemia. The results of 
the endocrinological studies (thyroid function, serum growth 
hormone, prolactin, cortisol, luteinizing hormone, and follicle- 
stimulating hormone levels) were normal; EEG and MRI of the 
brain and spinal cord were also normal. Electrocardiogram 
showed a right bundle-branch block. Pulmonary function tests 
showed moderate restrictive and mild obstructive tung disease. 
EMG studies were performed both with and without general anes- 
thesia. Motor and sensory nerve conduction studies were normal. 
Needle electrode examination of the right upper- and lower- 
extremity muscles revealed continuous motor muscle fiber activity 
mixed with a full interference pattern, which was completely 
abolished under general anesthesia. 
Throughout hospitalization, diazepam and baclofen were 
continued. She developed more frequent, severe, painful spasms 
accompanied by autonomic hyperactivity, including diffuse 
diaphoresis, agitation, pupillary dilatation, tachycardia to 180/min, 
arterial hypertension to 150/100 mmHg, hyperthermia to 37.4°C, 
and apnea with cyanosis lasting up to 60 s. A transient loss of con- 
sciousness during these episodes was noted on a few occasions. Re- 
peat EEGs were normal. The patient was found dead on the 26th 
day of hospitalization.

Immunological studies 
Autoantibodies directed against the central nervous system were 
investigated using immunoperoxidase staining of fixed rat brain 
and human cerebral cortex sections as previously described [33]. 
Postmortem blood and CSF of case 1 and serum and CSF of case 2 
were used as the sources of primary antibodies. GABA-NA were 
detected in postmortem blood of case i at a dilution 1 : 2 (Fig. 3) 
and in the serum of case 2 at a dilution of 1 : 50 (Fig. 4A). Screen- 
ing of a large number of control sera at 1 : 2 dilution demonstrated 
that immunoreactivity directed against GABA-NA was very spe- 
cific. GABA-NA were also detected in the CSF of case 2 at a dilu- 
tion of 1 : 10 (Fig. 4B) but not in the postmortem CSF of case 1. To 
identify the brain antigens against which GABA-NA of the two 
patients were directed, postmortem blood of case i and serum and 
CSF of case 2 were analyzed by immunoblot on total homogenate 
proteins of rat brain, as previously described [33]. Both serum and 
CSF of case 2 recognized a band with the electrophoretic mobility 
of glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) (Fig. 5), while postmortem 
blood of case i used at 1 : 100 dilution failed to recognize any band. 
The results of serum GABA-NA studies in healthy and diseased 
controls are available elsewhere [35]. 
Serum of case 2 was positive for islet-cell and gastric parietal- 
cell antibodies when tested by the standard assay for such anti- 
bodies. A search for organ-specific autoantibodies in the case 1 
was not possible because of the limited amount of postmortem 
material available. 
Fig.4A, B. Immunoperoxidase staining of rat cerebellar cortex 
using the serum (A) and the CSF (B) of case 2. GABA-ergic nerve 
terminals are darkly stained, strikingly at the base of Purkinje cells 
corresponding to basket cells (arrows), similarly at nerve terminals 
in the molecular layer and at rosettes of nerve terminals in the 
glomeruli of the granular layer (arrowheads). Note the identical 
staining pattern with the serum and the CSF 
No abnormalities were noted in a general autopsy except for 
mild arteriolar nephrosclerosis. Gross examination showed no ab- 
normality of the brain and spinal cord. Microscopic examination 
revealed multifocal mild lymphocytic perivascular infiltration in 
the spinal cord, brain stem, and basal ganglia (Fig. 2), but not in 
Discussion 
Clinical, immunological and autopsy findings 
The diagnosis of SMS is based on clinical features, and 
the diagnostic criteria proposed by Gordon et al. [9] in 
1967 remain useful [18]. Our patients satisfied these 
criteria, including prodromes characterized by episodic 
aching and tightness of the axial musculature with gradual 
spreading to limb muscles; progression of the symptoms 
with continuous, board-like stiffness or rigidity involving 
bilateral limb, trunk, and neck musculature; sudden ex- 
cruciatingly painful muscle spasms triggered by pre- 
cipitating factors; EMG findings showing continuously 
muscle fiber activity that was abolished by general anes- 
thesia; and exclusion of etiologies other than SMS. 
SMS has been previously described in association 
with a variety of disorders including epilepsy [21, 33, 34],

94 
dementia [4], pontine atrophy with CSF abnormality 
[20], cancer [27], paraneoplastic syndrome [22], and 
malabsorption syndrome [29]. However, the most con- 
sistent association has been found between SMS and 
organ-specific autoimmune diseases such as insulin- 
dependent diabetes mellitus [6, 18, 41], hyper- and 
hypothyroidism [7, 11, 35, 36], vitiligo, and pernicious 
anemia [35, 41]. The association with insulin-dependent 
diabetes mellitus is the most frequently observed [33]. 
Our case 1 had insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus and 
case 2 was positive both for islet-cell antibodies and for 
gastric parietal-cell antibodies. In both patients, sera 
were positive for GABA-NA. GABA-NA are present in 
at least 60% of the patients with SMS [35]. In case 2, 
similar autoantibodies were also present in high concen- 
trations in the CSF, and immunoblot analysis identified 
GAD as the major autoantigen. A high specificity of 
GABA-NA to SMS was also shown in recent studies 
[35]. An abnormal IgG index [37] and oligoclonal bands 
were found in the CSF of the same patient. These find- 
ings all suggest that there is an immune-mediated pro- 
cess that might impair GABA-ergic neurons. This pro- 
cess may have led to the disease in our two patients. 
Detailed neuropathological studies of SMS have been 
meager and, when available, have shown no specific 
changes (Table 1) [8, 19, 23, 24, 38, 39]. Autopsy studies 
showed perivascular gliosis in case 1 and perivascular 
lymphocytic infiltration in case 2. While these histo- 
logical changes found in our patients are relatively non- 
specific, the lymphocytic infiltration observed in case 2 
supports the hypothesis of an autoimmune origin of the 
disease. It cannot be excluded that the perivascular 
gliosis observed in case 1 might represent the sequela of 
a previous active lymphocytic infiltration. In fact, no 
GABA-NA were found in the CSF of this patient and 
the GABA-NA levels in the blood were very low. In 
contrast, the levels of GABA-NA observed both in the 
serum and the CSF of case 2 were the highest of a rela- 
tively large group of SMS patients recently studied by us 
[35]. (Alternatively, the low titer of GABA-NA in case 1 
could be related to the fact that both blood and CSF for 
GABA-NA analysis were obtained postmortem.) Peri- 
vascular lymphocytic inflammation similar to that ob- 
served in case 2 has been described in cases of encephalo- 
myelitis with rigidity [12, 14, 17, 40] or of subacute myo- 
clonic spinal neuronitis [2] (Table 1). Muscle rigidity and 
painful spasms in these patients closely resemble those in 
SMS. The autopsy findings in case 2 suggest that, as pre- 
viously proposed by Kasperek and Zebrowski [14], at 
least some cases of SMS and encephalomyelitis with 
rigidity may undergo the same disease process. 
Autonomic dysfunction 
Our patients had paroxysmal attacks of transient arterial 
hypertension, hyperpyrexia, tachycardia, pupillary dila-

stimulating hormone levels) were normal; EEG and MRI of the 
brain and spinal cord were also normal. Electrocardiogram 
showed a right bundle-branch block. Pulmonary function tests 
showed moderate restrictive and mild obstructive tung disease. 
EMG studies were performed both with and without general anes- 
thesia. Motor and sensory nerve conduction studies were normal. 
Needle electrode examination of the right upper- and lower- 
extremity muscles revealed continuous motor muscle fiber activity 
mixed with a full interference pattern, which was completely 
abolished under general anesthesia. 
Throughout hospitalization, diazepam and baclofen were 
continued. She developed more frequent, severe, painful spasms 
accompanied by autonomic hyperactivity, including diffuse 
diaphoresis, agitation, pupillary dilatation, tachycardia to 180/min, 
arterial hypertension to 150/100 mmHg, hyperthermia to 37.4°C, 
and apnea with cyanosis lasting up to 60 s. A transient loss of con- 
sciousness during these episodes was noted on a few occasions. Re- 
peat EEGs were normal. The patient was found dead on the 26th 
day of hospitalization.

Immunological studies 
Autoantibodies directed against the central nervous system were 
investigated using immunoperoxidase staining of fixed rat brain 
and human cerebral cortex sections as previously described [33]. 
Postmortem blood and CSF of case 1 and serum and CSF of case 2 
were used as the sources of primary antibodies. GABA-NA were 
detected in postmortem blood of case i at a dilution 1 : 2 (Fig. 3) 
and in the serum of case 2 at a dilution of 1 : 50 (Fig. 4A). Screen- 
ing of a large number of control sera at 1 : 2 dilution demonstrated 
that immunoreactivity directed against GABA-NA was very spe- 
cific. GABA-NA were also detected in the CSF of case 2 at a dilu- 
tion of 1 : 10 (Fig. 4B) but not in the postmortem CSF of case 1. To 
identify the brain antigens against which GABA-NA of the two 
patients were directed, postmortem blood of case i and serum and 
CSF of case 2 were analyzed by immunoblot on total homogenate 
proteins of rat brain, as previously described [33]. Both serum and 
CSF of case 2 recognized a band with the electrophoretic mobility 
of glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) (Fig. 5), while postmortem 
blood of case i used at 1 : 100 dilution failed to recognize any band. 
The results of serum GABA-NA studies in healthy and diseased 
controls are available elsewhere [35]. 
Serum of case 2 was positive for islet-cell and gastric parietal- 
cell antibodies when tested by the standard assay for such anti- 
bodies. A search for organ-specific autoantibodies in the case 1 
was not possible because of the limited amount of postmortem 
material available.

Discussion 
Clinical, immunological and autopsy findings 
The diagnosis of SMS is based on clinical features, and 
the diagnostic criteria proposed by Gordon et al. [9] in 
1967 remain useful [18]. Our patients satisfied these 
criteria, including prodromes characterized by episodic 
aching and tightness of the axial musculature with gradual 
spreading to limb muscles; progression of the symptoms 
with continuous, board-like stiffness or rigidity involving 
bilateral limb, trunk, and neck musculature; sudden ex- 
cruciatingly painful muscle spasms triggered by pre- 
cipitating factors; EMG findings showing continuously 
muscle fiber activity that was abolished by general anes- 
thesia; and exclusion of etiologies other than SMS. 
SMS has been previously described in association 
with a variety of disorders including epilepsy [21, 33, 34],

94 
dementia [4], pontine atrophy with CSF abnormality 
[20], cancer [27], paraneoplastic syndrome [22], and 
malabsorption syndrome [29]. However, the most con- 
sistent association has been found between SMS and 
organ-specific autoimmune diseases such as insulin- 
dependent diabetes mellitus [6, 18, 41], hyper- and 
hypothyroidism [7, 11, 35, 36], vitiligo, and pernicious 
anemia [35, 41]. The association with insulin-dependent 
diabetes mellitus is the most frequently observed [33]. 
Our case 1 had insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus and 
case 2 was positive both for islet-cell antibodies and for 
gastric parietal-cell antibodies. In both patients, sera 
were positive for GABA-NA. GABA-NA are present in 
at least 60% of the patients with SMS [35]. In case 2, 
similar autoantibodies were also present in high concen- 
trations in the CSF, and immunoblot analysis identified 
GAD as the major autoantigen. A high specificity of 
GABA-NA to SMS was also shown in recent studies 
[35]. An abnormal IgG index [37] and oligoclonal bands 
were found in the CSF of the same patient. These find- 
ings all suggest that there is an immune-mediated pro- 
cess that might impair GABA-ergic neurons. This pro- 
cess may have led to the disease in our two patients. 
Detailed neuropathological studies of SMS have been 
meager and, when available, have shown no specific 
changes (Table 1) [8, 19, 23, 24, 38, 39]. Autopsy studies 
showed perivascular gliosis in case 1 and perivascular 
lymphocytic infiltration in case 2. While these histo- 
logical changes found in our patients are relatively non- 
specific, the lymphocytic infiltration observed in case 2 
supports the hypothesis of an autoimmune origin of the 
disease. It cannot be excluded that the perivascular 
gliosis observed in case 1 might represent the sequela of 
a previous active lymphocytic infiltration. In fact, no 
GABA-NA were found in the CSF of this patient and 
the GABA-NA levels in the blood were very low. In 
contrast, the levels of GABA-NA observed both in the 
serum and the CSF of case 2 were the highest of a rela- 
tively large group of SMS patients recently studied by us 
[35]. (Alternatively, the low titer of GABA-NA in case 1 
could be related to the fact that both blood and CSF for 
GABA-NA analysis were obtained postmortem.) Peri- 
vascular lymphocytic inflammation similar to that ob- 
served in case 2 has been described in cases of encephalo- 
myelitis with rigidity [12, 14, 17, 40] or of subacute myo- 
clonic spinal neuronitis [2] (Table 1). Muscle rigidity and 
painful spasms in these patients closely resemble those in 
SMS. The autopsy findings in case 2 suggest that, as pre- 
viously proposed by Kasperek and Zebrowski [14], at 
least some cases of SMS and encephalomyelitis with 
rigidity may undergo the same disease process.
